analysis.title: Anatomy Of A Crash – Lessons From Dotcom
key_insights: TS Lombard (Dario Perkins) does not think the AI boom has ended and sees reasons for a rebound. The note argues the first year of the Dotcom crash calls for humility and finds troubling parallels with summer 2000, just before that crash.

Reasons given for the boom to continue: hyperscalers have not yet cut their strong capex plans, compute demand is solid as shown by GPU rental prices, the Fed has only just started a new tightening cycle, and a market correction with a prompt rebound usually comes before the ultimate crash.

The Nasdaq peaked on 10 March 2000 and was down over a third by mid-April. The trigger remains unclear. Contributing factors were Fed tightening (25bp in February, 25bp in March, 50bp in May), worry about unprofitable dotcoms (Barron's 'Burning Fast' cover story), and a wave of IPO lockup expiries with insiders selling.

The Nasdaq rebounded 35% from its lows by mid-June 2000, leaving it 15% below the March peak. Drivers were dip-buying, the view that rate hikes no longer mattered for tech, rotation into profitable names (Cisco, Oracle, Sun, Intel, Microsoft), and a strong dollar.
Fed staff published a study at the Nasdaq's early-summer 2000 peak that supported the market consensus that tech was relatively immune to higher interest rates.

In autumn 2000 the Nasdaq broke its previous lows by mid-October and ended the year at roughly half its March peak, a fall of more than 40% in three months. The selloff began in unprofitable dotcoms and spread to profitable suppliers (Cisco, Lucent, Nortel, Sun, Oracle) because the dotcoms were their customers.

Venture and IPO funding tightened through 2000 and credit spreads widened, cutting off funding for weaker firms. Earnings misses then cascaded through the tech ecosystem. A roughly 35% oil price jump in summer 2000 and a weakening macro economy added pressure.

Lags in the tech supply chain (orders, backlogs and capex plans taking months to adjust) let bellwethers keep posting strong results while the crash developed. Within six months shortages turned into a glut.

The Fed saw a recession risk by the November and December 2000 meetings, but Greenspan still treated the weakness as a soft patch and an inventory overhang, even at the May 2001 meeting. The NBER dates the recession from March 2001.

Corporate earnings for the late 1990s were revised down in 2004 because the BEA treats exercised stock options as labour income. TS Lombard says financial engineering, vendor financing and fraud were also present then. It thinks a similar problem today is possible to a smaller degree, but the 'E' in the PE is more likely the unsustainable part than the 'P'.

Lessons: buy-the-dip works until it does not, seeing a technology in real life does not rule out a bubble, and 'Fed hikes don't matter' was the consensus at the Dotcom peak and was wrong. Stress starts in the weakest part of the ecosystem and spreads to the core, and bottlenecks can precede a glut.
Six months into the Nasdaq correction the S&P 500 was still at all-time highs. Broad indices came under serious pressure only when the economic outlook soured.

One silver lining is that consumption never contracted after the 2000 crash despite the stock collapse. TS Lombard attributes this partly to housing responding quickly to Fed cuts, and expects a similar result if the Fed cuts rapidly into an eventual AI crash.

sector_views.rationale: Constructive near term, with a possible rebound, but the Dotcom parallels call for humility and an eventual AI crash is the base case in its wider research.

earnings_insights: Q2 2000 tech earnings were strong but Q3 2000 estimates came under pressure by the September reporting season, which preceded the autumn leg lower.

BEA revisions in early 2004 turned late-1990s corporate earnings from rapid growth into stagnation, because exercised stock options are treated as labour income. The note says the corporate profit share may be overstated today if similar distortions exist.

macro_indicators.interpretation: A faster hiking pace in early 2000 contributed to the Nasdaq's initial selloff. The note draws a parallel with the Fed's new tightening cycle today.
The hiking cycle started in the second half of 1999 before the pace stepped up in 2000.
The energy price surge squeezed real incomes and added to the macro deterioration during the Dotcom crash.
TS Lombard lists the early stage of tightening as a reason the AI boom may continue, while noting that 'Fed hikes don't matter' was wrong in 2000.

risk_factors: Hyperscalers could downgrade their capex plans. Compute demand could weaken. Both are currently cited as supports for the AI boom.
Supply chain lags can hide weakening demand, so strong bellwether results may precede a glut.
Tighter financial conditions and credit stress can cut off funding to weaker AI-ecosystem firms, then spread to profitable core companies.
Earnings downgrades can arrive after stocks are already under heavy selling pressure.
Economists and central banks tend to see recessions late and adjust forecasts incrementally.
Corporate profits may be overstated, so the 'E' in PE may be unsustainable.

tension_points.bull_case: Hyperscalers have not downgraded capex plans, GPU rental prices show solid compute demand, the Fed has only just started tightening, and a correction followed by a prompt rebound often comes before the ultimate crash.
tension_points.bear_case: The same arguments were made as the Dotcom bubble burst. In 2000 dip-buying, 'rate hikes don't matter' and supply-chain bottlenecks all preceded a crash that spread from weak firms to profitable core companies.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Hyperscaler capex downgrades or earnings downgrades across the AI supply chain, since in 2000 the crash became unstoppable once earnings expectations came under sustained pressure.

theme_stances.key_argument: The arguments for the AI boom continuing are eerily similar to those made as the Dotcom bubble burst, which calls for humility.
theme_stances.evidence: eerily similar to the arguments people were making as the Dotcom bubble burst

theme_stances.key_argument: 'Fed hikes don't matter' was the consensus at the Dotcom peak and turned out to be wrong.
